Similar Bedrock/Java-aware world-folder-set logic, but with rollback: pre-checks that none of the target names already exist, moves each region folder in turn, and if any single move fails, walks movedPairs.reversed() to move already-renamed folders back before reporting failure -- genuine transactional-rename logic worth preserving precisely.
Shells out to /usr/bin/unzip (-t to validate, -o -d to extract) and wraps FileManager copy for the 'existing folder' source case; shared by replaceWorld. Subprocess-driving I/O, agent.

Resolves/creates the Application Support directory, and on existing config: does a one-time plaintext-to-Keychain migration for the old remote_api_token and per-server xbox_broadcast_alt_password JSON keys (reading raw JSON directly, since the typed AppConfig no longer carries them), decodes AppConfig, clamps remoteAPIPort to a valid range, then populates secrets from Keychain. On decode failure (R3), preserves the corrupt file as a timestamped .corrupt-<ts> copy before falling back to defaults, recording the path for a one-time user alert. This is real config-lifecycle and pairing-token migration policy -- must be preserved exactly to avoid silently losing a user's Remote API token or Xbox passwords on first Rust-agent run against an existing config file.

Re-reads config.json from disk (or resets to defaults if the file vanished), re-clamps remoteAPIPort, and re-populates Keychain-backed secrets. Distinct from init in that it has no migration/corruption-recovery path -- agent-owned disk-sync workflow.

Before writing JSON: persists the in-memory Remote API token to Keychain, and if no token exists anywhere yet, generates a fresh one (AppConfig.generateRemoteAPIToken) and writes it to Keychain -- this is literally the pairing-token lifecycle the deletion test calls out as agent-owned. Also persists every server's Xbox broadcast alt-password to Keychain. Then atomically encodes+writes config.json (pretty-printed, sorted keys) and fires onSaveError at most once per session on failure.

Hydrates the in-memory config's Remote API token and each server's Xbox alt-password from Keychain after every decode/reload; generates+stores a brand-new token if none exists (first install case). JSON intentionally omits these fields -- Keychain is the source of truth, and this is the rehydration step that makes that split work. Directly relevant to the agent's pairing/token design.

Lists installed Java or Bedrock packs via ResourcePackManager, determines Geyser availability/pack list for Java servers, and if a Java pack is marked active, ensures the local HTTP host server is actually serving it (self-healing sync between on-disk state and the running host). Real state-reconciliation workflow.

NSOpenPanel presentation filtered by content type (.zip, or .mcpack/.zip for Bedrock/Geyser) that immediately delegates to installResourcePack/installGeyserPack with no logic of its own beyond picking the file -- pure Finder/file-picker presentation per the deletion test.

Validates Java packs must be .zip (rejects other extensions with a user-facing error) before delegating to ResourcePackManager.installJavaPack/installBedrockPack/installGeyserPack off the main thread, then refreshes state. Real format-gatekeeping, agent.

Delegates removal/enable-toggle to ResourcePackManager, but also stops the resource-pack HTTP host server when the currently-hosted active Java pack is the one removed -- a real cross-component consequence beyond a plain delegate call.

Deactivation clears the active-pack fields and stops the local host. Activation requires a public-facing host address (DuckDNS hostname, else cached public IP -- resourcePackHostAddress's own policy) and errors out with a specific user-facing message if none is available; otherwise computes the pack's SHA1, builds a percent-encoded public download URL, starts an embedded HTTP file server (resourcePackHostServer) bound to the server's configured port, and writes url+sha1+require into the server.properties-equivalent config. This is a real embedded-server-plus-protocol workflow (Java's resource-pack-url/resource-pack-sha1/require-resource-pack mechanism), squarely agent.

Starts (or restarts, if the bound port drifted from the configured one) the local HTTP host serving the Java packs directory; called both on pack-list reload and on server start so joining players can always fetch the active pack.

DECIDED (agent) -- always forward TCP for Java; only add UDP when Bedrock/Geyser is enabled, and which port(s) to mention. This is domain knowledge tied directly to the server's own configuration (server type, Geyser enabled or not), the same class of thing as the settings schema (agent-owned, client-rendered) -- it belongs next to the config it depends on so every client gets consistent, correctly-derived guidance instead of re-implementing the Java/Bedrock/Geyser port-selection rule themselves. Producing a display string rather than persisted state doesn't change that; the settings schema itself is 'just' a display structure too. Decided agent.

Sets selectedServer to switch the sidebar/detail pane -- pure navigation state, matches the deletion test's 'window and navigation state -> Client' row.

Predicate checking whether a given ConfigServer is the currently active *and* running server -- small, but it's the real guard UI uses to prevent destructive conversion actions on a live server (mirrors the same running-server guard duplicated inline in replaceWorld/renameWorld in the WorldManagement file).

The full Bedrock<->Java conversion pipeline: resolves the Java path and confirms Chunker is installed (ChunkerManager, not in this file), validates the target slot name, unzips the source slot to a unique temp dir (via /usr/bin/unzip, deliberately using FileHandle.nullDevice instead of Pipe() to avoid a deadlock on large worlds -- a subtle, must-preserve detail), locates the actual world folder inside the extracted content, runs the Chunker CLI conversion, packages the output into a slot-compatible zip, places it into either a brand-new WorldSlot or an existing one being overwritten (writing slot metadata + zip size via WorldSlotManager), takes a pre-conversion backup of the target server's current world, activates the new slot, and finally navigates the UI to the target server -- with guaranteed temp-dir cleanup on every exit path (do/catch wrapping steps 1-8). This is the single largest, most I/O-driving workflow across all 8 files -- unambiguously agent.

Orchestrates building a .msctransfer package for every configured server: stages a temp dir, bundles paper.jar (Java), world_slots/backups/plugins/mods/resource-packs wholesale, libraries/ for NeoForge/Forge, live world folders (may be newer than the last slot zip), top-level config files filtered by extension, reads the Java port and Paper version sidecar for later conflict detection, sanitizes machine-specific paths (serverDir, paperJarPath, Xbox alt-account fields) out of the persisted server model, writes manifest.json, then zips via /usr/bin/zip. Definitionally an agent workflow -- multi-step file staging + process launch that must produce byte-identical package layout for any future importer to consume.

Unzips a package, decodes manifest.json, rejects manifests from a newer formatVersion than this build supports, then for every entry compares its recorded Java/Bedrock port against the ports already in use by locally-configured servers and flags conflicts with a human-readable detail string. The port-conflict detection is a real policy decision (not just I/O) that the agent must replicate so any client driving an import gets the same conflict warnings before committing.

Applies a previously-inspected import plan: for each manifest entry, picks a non-colliding destination folder, restores configs/world_slots/backups/plugins/mods/resource-packs/libraries from the staged package, restores paper.jar only if it was bundled, rewrites server.properties' server-port when the caller supplied a port override, builds a fresh ConfigServer (new id, re-rooted paths), restores live world folders when present or falls back to activating the recorded active world slot, and on replaceAll mode wipes existing servers' Keychain secrets before replacing the server list. Genuine multi-step orchestration with real precedence rules (live world > slot restore) -- agent.

Shared low-level helpers deliberately kept non-isolated so background Task.detached closures can call them: folder-name sanitization + de-duplication for package layout, a line-oriented rewrite of server.properties' server-port= line, and thin wrappers around /usr/bin/zip and /usr/bin/unzip. All four are process-launch/file-mutation primitives the export/import workflows depend on -- agent, not client presentation.

Static rule set that decides what does and doesn't get bundled into a transfer package (which top-level dirs are always excluded -- logs/cache/versions/live world dirs superseded by world_slots -- and which file extensions count as a 'config file' to copy into configs/), plus the format-version gate inspectTransferPackage enforces. This is the actual definition of what a transfer package contains, not incidental constant declarations -- agent must encode the same rules to stay interoperable.

Resolves a candidate java binary (configured path first, falling back to PATH via `which`), launches `java -version` (which writes to stderr), extracts the major version with a regex handling both modern ("21.0.3") and legacy 1.x ("1.8.0_281" -> 8) formats, and classifies the result into ready/attention(<21)/attention(<17 -- unsupported)/missing. This is exactly the 'Server installation detection' example the deletion test calls out as Agent -- any client needs the host machine's actual Java state, which only the agent process running on that machine can determine.

DECIDED (agent) -- checks for the Tailscale.app bundle/CLI at known paths, then scans network interfaces via getifaddrs/getnameinfo for a 100.x.x.x (Tailscale CGNAT range) address. The two framings aren't actually symmetric: a client checking its own Tailscale status answers 'is this device on the tailnet,' but what matters for reachability is 'is the *agent's* host on the tailnet' -- a question only the agent can answer about itself. Decided agent.

Static launch-time gate: given the set of configured server types, decides whether any critical dependency (currently just Java, when a Java server is configured) is missing, via a `which java` check. Used by the macOS app to decide whether to auto-show this screen at launch -- the auto-show decision itself is client UI flow, but the underlying is-java-installed check is the same agent-owned detection as detectJava/isJavaInstalled above and must exist as an agent capability regardless of which client asks.

Java player-profile load pipeline: scans playerdata/*.dat off-main via PlayerDataManager, applies usercache.json and ops.json to fill in usernames/op status, marks online state from the live player list, loads the hidden-UUID sets so isProfileHidden() works immediately, then kicks off async Mojang UUID resolution for anything still unresolved. Multi-step orchestration over on-disk state -- agent.

Bedrock equivalent: scans the LevelDB off-main via BedrockPlayerDataManager (NBT parsed during scan), loads hidden Bedrock/Java lists, applies the persisted BedrockNameCache (overwriting even 'Unknown Player' placeholders so manual/auto-resolved names stick), marks online state by XUID or by matched live gamertag, then queues batched XUID->gamertag and Floodgate-UUID resolution. Agent -- this is the authoritative player-identity pipeline for Bedrock servers.

A distinct classification rule embedded inline (lines ~186-209, not its own function): broadcast/transfer joins land on disk as anonymous `server_<uuid>` records sharing no identifier with the live console identity. The rule correlates by liveness instead -- if exactly one unresolved `server_` profile exists and exactly one live gamertag has no matching profile yet, they must be the same player, so the name is bound and cached against the stable `server_<uuid>` key; ambiguous cases (multiple unknowns at once) are deliberately left unresolved for manual identification. Called out separately because it's easy to lose during porting -- it's inline logic, not a named symbol, and its correctness (exactly-one-to-exactly-one matching) is load-bearing for correct Realm/Floodgate player identification.

Batched (5 at a time, 250ms between batches to respect rate limits), concurrent (withTaskGroup) resolution of Bedrock XUID -> gamertag and gamertag -> Floodgate UUID via BedrockPlayerDataManager, writing resolved names back into the persisted BedrockNameCache so they survive log rollovers and future sessions. Network + cache-write workflow -- agent.

Manual-identification action: trims and validates a user-supplied gamertag, persists it to bedrock_names.json via BedrockNameCache.record (so the assignment survives restarts and self-heals if the console log later confirms it), updates in-memory state, and kicks off async Floodgate UUID resolution for the newly-named profile. Real validation + persistence, not pure forwarding -- agent.

Batched (5 at a time, 250ms apart) Mojang session-server lookups (sessionserver.mojang.com/session/minecraft/profile/<uuid>) with a custom User-Agent and 10s timeout, decoding the JSON {name} response. This is the Java-edition analog of the Bedrock XUID resolution above -- an external API integration + small JSON parser, agent-owned.

The player-data mutation surface: computes a name's offline-mode UUID and copies .dat -> that target (the documented 'key action when switching online mode -> offline mode'), copies onto an arbitrary target UUID, copies one player's data onto another's UUID (overwrite), deletes a .dat permanently, and duplicates a .dat under a fresh random UUID. Each is a thin sequence over PlayerDataManager plus a log line and a profile-list refresh, but together they constitute the actual player-data mutation API the agent must expose -- not a client rendering concern, and each encodes a specific real rule (e.g. which UUID a migration targets) rather than being pure glue.

DECIDED (agent) -- skin-override management: resolves display appearance via PlayerSkinStore, lets a user override the lookup identifier for a profile, saves an uploaded skin to server-side storage, clears an override. Persistence (override JSON + skin file under the server directory) is agent-owned, full stop -- it's part of the player-profile record the agent serves to every client. The NSImage parameter is an implementation-boundary detail, not a disposition question: the port replaces it with a raw-bytes upload boundary (client picks/crops if it wants, sends bytes; agent validates and stores).

DECIDED (agent) -- the full catalog of Minecraft server commands: name, description, category, positional argument shape, and which of Java/Bedrock each command supports. `commands(for:)` filters by server type. Duplicating this catalog per-client is exactly the drift MSC 2 exists to eliminate (D-005) -- a Java-only command list that goes stale in one client but not another is a real support-burden bug waiting to happen, and 'which commands does this server accept' is genuinely per-server-type domain knowledge, the same class as the settings schema (agent/schema, client-rendered). CommandCategory.icon/color (SwiftUI Color/SF Symbol) stay excluded as pure client rendering. Decided agent, not duplicated static data.

DECIDED (agent) -- the autocomplete engine: tokenizes input, decides whether the cursor is completing a command name or filling an argument slot, filters online players by prefix for playerName slots and the fixed option list by prefix for keyword slots, returns up to 6 completions. Same reasoning as the catalog itself (row above) plus one more reason unique to this function: it needs the live online-player list, which is inherently fresher and cheaper to filter where it already lives (the agent) than to ship the full roster to every client for local filtering. Decided agent.

Imports an existing server folder or .zip into MSC: sanitizes the display name into a safe folder name, copies or extracts (via /usr/bin/ditto, chosen specifically to avoid /usr/bin/unzip's mode-000 quirk on user-supplied archives) into the servers root, unwraps a single top-level folder if the zip had one, detects Java flavor, reads/overrides server.properties or bedrock properties (port/max-players/level-name), writes eula.txt if the user accepted it in the wizard, builds the ConfigServer, creates an initial world slot from whatever world data was found, and registers + activates the server. Canonical agent workflow -- process launch, file staging, config mutation, and multi-step orchestration.

Pre-import inspection so the wizard can show the user what will be imported before anything is copied: detects server type from file signatures (a .jar means Java, bedrock_server/.exe means Bedrock), reads port/max-players/EULA status, and scans for world folders under both a worlds/ subdirectory and the server root (any dir containing level.dat, skipping known non-world dirs). Groups vanilla dimension companions (_nether/_the_end) into their root world by name pattern, detects inline Nether/End via DIM-1/DIM1 folders, and sums size across root + companions. This is 'Server installation detection' verbatim from the deletion test's Agent column.

Signature-based Java server flavor detector, checked in priority order: NeoForge (via libraries/net/neoforged/neoforge/<ver>/unix_args.txt, delegating MC-version lookup to NeoForgeInstaller), Forge (libraries/net/minecraftforge/forge/<mc>-<ver>/unix_args.txt, MC version split from the dir name), Fabric (fabric-server-launch*.jar + loader version from .fabric/.../fabric-loader/), then jar-prefix matching for Purpur/vanilla/Paper (default fallback) with MC-version extraction from filename stems (strips a trailing numeric -build suffix). Shared by both importExistingServer and scanServerDirectory -- a real detection policy the agent must own to install/manage any given server correctly.

Decides the host and port Xbox Broadcast advertises to joining clients: a per-server manual override wins outright; otherwise when playit.gg is enabled and a Bedrock tunnel address is stored, that tunnel's host/port is used (stripped/parsed from 'host:port'); otherwise falls back through DuckDNS hostname -> cached public IP -> local IP depending on the server's XboxBroadcastIPMode (auto/publicIP/privateIP). Getting this wrong sends players to a dead endpoint (the file's own comments flag this exact failure mode for the port half) -- a real precedence policy, agent-owned.

Signs out of the current Xbox broadcast account: stops any running Java/Bedrock broadcaster so the auth cache isn't held open, then deletes the cache/ directory holding the OAuth device-code token so the next start forces a fresh sign-in. Token-lifecycle management -- the same category the deletion test names for pairing tokens -- agent.

Persists a server's broadcast profile: trims and nil-normalizes email/gamertag/avatar-path fields, writes the alt-account password to Keychain (never to the plain config), and re-syncs the on-disk broadcaster config afterward. saveBroadcastGamertagFromPrompt is the write-back half of the save-gamertag flow below. Credential handling + config-file resync -- agent.

notes: Manual process-lifecycle controls for both broadcaster variants (MCXboxBroadcast for Java, the same JAR reused for Bedrock): validates JAR/config prerequisites, launches or terminates the helper process, and surfaces structured errors (already-running vs. failed-to-start). Process launch/lifecycle -- agent, not view code, even though today it's triggered from sidebar buttons.

Delayed auto-start orchestration (15s for Bedrock, 30s for Java) gated by a stack of guard conditions re-checked after the delay: auto-start preference enabled, per-server broadcast enabled, not already running, server still the active running server, stop not requested, and not mid first-run Initiate (which has its own completion flow that would race a broadcaster popping up). This guard stack is exactly the kind of orchestration logic that has to survive the port correctly or broadcasters will start at the wrong time -- agent.
Opens the broadcast config directory in Finder (NSWorkspace-style openInFinder). This is the deletion test's own 'Finder / file-picker presentation -> Client' example, verbatim.

That dedup state has no meaning persisted server-side or shared across clients -- it's definitionally per-UI-session. Confirmed client, not reopened.

This is verbatim the deletion test's 'Console log parsing -> Agent' example.

This classification scheme is reusable business logic any client's console view would want consistently, distinct from the raw parsing above -- agent.

Resolve-once-with-cache wrapper around the pure AddonUpdateResolver: no-ops when the cached plan is already current for this server and force==false (so calling it on every Components-tab appear is cheap), otherwise resolves and merges resolver-discovered links into the persisted config. Agent.

The core install/update pipeline: downloads the target Modrinth version's primary file, preserves the add-on's enabled/disabled state by mirroring the '.disabled' filename suffix onto the new file, removes the old jar when the filename changed, computes and persists the new SHA-512, and pulls newly-required dependencies. updateAddons sequences this dependency-aware batch over multiple selected items with one refresh at the end. Real download+install+state-preservation workflow -- agent.

Associates a user-picked Modrinth project with an unlinked installed file (provenance .userLinked, so mergeDiscoveredLinks above won't overwrite it), persists, and re-resolves so update status appears. Agent.

Repairs an 'incompatible version' startup problem: identifies the Modrinth project via the persisted AddonLink first, falling back to hashing the installed file and looking it up by SHA-512; finds the best version compatible with the server's loader + Minecraft version; downloads it preserving the disabled-suffix convention from applyAddonUpdate; removes the old jar; and pulls newly-required dependencies. Agent.

Repairs a 'missing dependency' startup problem: since the dependency isn't installed, its identity can only come from the known-alias table + a Modrinth search (the hash/persisted-link rungs don't apply -- there's no file yet), with a fallback chain (canonical-slug match -> normalized-slug match -> title match -> first hit) before installing via the shared install path. Agent.

FLAG -- a documented four-tier identity-resolution ladder for 'View on Modrinth': (a) installed file's SHA-512 -> Modrinth version -> project (most authoritative), (b) a persisted AddonLink matched by filename, (c) the known-alias table trusted as a real slug, (d) a Modrinth search on the canonical query, with a bare-canonical-slug floor so the UI always has something to open. repairIncompatibleAddon and installMissingDependency each reimplement a similar-but-not-identical ladder rather than calling this one -- likely organic drift worth consolidating into one shared resolver during the Rust port.

Extracts a dropped/browsed .zip via a /usr/bin/ditto subprocess into a temp dir (avoids /usr/bin/unzip's mode-000 quirk on user files), unwraps a single-root-folder zip layout, then hands the resolved directory to scanServerDirectory for detection. The zip-staging + unwrap logic is real import workflow the agent must reproduce even though the actual directory scan is implemented elsewhere.

Classifies a dropped/browsed file as a modpack (.mrpack, or .zip sniffed via AppViewModel.readCurseForgeMetadata) vs an existing-server import, then dispatches to processModpackURL or performScan accordingly. This classification decision belongs to server-installation detection, not UI.

Given a staged .mrpack/CurseForge .zip/folder/plain-zip, pins the wizard's flavor+category+version from parsed pack metadata (readMrpackMetadata / readCurseForgeMetadata, defined elsewhere), stages the item(s) in stagedAddOns for install-after-creation, and derives status text. The staging decision workflow -- what to do with parsed metadata -- lives here even though the parsers themselves are elsewhere.

Idempotency-checked component provisioning: scans the plugin template dir for geyser+floodgate jar name patterns, and if enabling cross-play with jars missing, downloads both (via viewModel.downloadLatestGeyserTemplate/FloodgateTemplate) then re-verifies presence to report success/failure. Component-installation-detection domain.

Guards on viewModel.isXboxBroadcastHelperInstalled before triggering downloadOrUpdateXboxBroadcastJar -- an idempotency check on top of an agent-owned download, same pattern as the cross-play row above.

Confirmed client.

Builds the Remote API's valid-token map: owner token from Keychain plus remoteAPISharedAccess entries filtered by isExpired, mapped to admin/guest/named permission roles. This is the pairing/token-lifecycle security policy the table calls out as Agent-owned explicitly.

This *is* the agent's local HTTP API contract the Rust port must replicate route-for-route.

Component-version-detection workflow: resolves installed Paper version via sidecar -> filename parse -> jar presence; scans plugins/ for Geyser/Floodgate jar names + parses trailing build numbers; fetches latest metadata concurrently; computes per-component up-to-date status; branches on installStep flavors (Forge/NeoForge args-file check) vs single-jar flavors.

Download-and-apply component-update workflow for paper/geyser/floodgate: downloads latest, writes the Paper version sidecar, and renames the jar file to reflect the new build number via renamedJar (line 1584) -- a small filename parser that swaps the trailing numeric build suffix.

Process-termination orchestration run on every server exit: captures initiation context before it's wiped, resets running-state/metrics, stops broadcast/auto-backup, fires stop notifications, calls diagnoseUnexpectedStop + crash-loop-guarded auto-restart scheduling (skipped during initiation passes), writes last_startup_result.json on an unclean stop, creates the initial world slot if needed, and routes initiation completion. Bedrock and VM-Bedrock share the same handler.

The console ingestion pipeline: a thread-safe line buffer fed from the backend's readabilityHandler thread, drained on a burst-adaptive cadence (100ms normal / 250ms during floods of >=100 pending lines), parsed off-main via ConsoleLineParser + ANSI stripping + ChatFeedParser, then committed on the main actor running the per-line side-effect scan (handleServerOutputLine) before appending to the console.

Detects a genuine misconfiguration -- playit tunnel enabled, Simple Voice Chat plugin installed, but its voice tunnel not enabled, and the prompt not yet dismissed -- to gate a one-time alert. Config-correctness policy, not just UI state.

Routes app-generated log lines into the console + Remote API SSE feed. noteCreation additionally buffers creation-time output so it survives the console-clear that happens on server selection, replaying it into the newly created server's console afterward -- real log-continuity behavior, not pure forwarding.

DECIDED (agent) -- the ordered sequence of state reloads on active-server switch: persists the new activeServerId, resets live metrics, reloads backups/world slots/resource packs/session log/player profiles/EULA/Geyser config/server settings/components snapshot/health cards, clears console, checks SVC mismatch. Most called methods forward to logic covered elsewhere, but the ordering itself -- e.g. console cleared before the SVC-mismatch check runs against it, avoiding a stale-console read -- is real sequencing behavior a headless agent's own 'switch active server' operation must reproduce for internal consistency, regardless of which client triggered the switch. Decided agent.
Resolves which world slot is "active" via a fallback chain: explicit active_slot_id.txt marker -> most-recently-played slot -> newest-created slot. Real resolution policy, not just a getter.

Determines whether the next start should run the "Initiate" (first-run) flow, using hasShownFirstStartPopup as authoritative with a fallback heuristic for imported/legacy servers: presence of generated world data (level.dat, or a Bedrock db/ folder) on disk. Arms a silent-consume flag so the auto-poll's spark reply block never reaches the visible console.

Schedules a repeating Timer that fires createAutoBackupForServer, but skips the backup entirely when no players are online (real policy, not just plumbing) and can be live-reconfigured (interval/enabled) while the server is running.

Reads/writes the playit.gg secret key via Keychain, including a one-time migration from a legacy plain-text file. Matches the deletion test's "pairing security and token lifecycle" example almost exactly, for a third-party service credential.

Resolves which local ports need tunneling: Java from server.properties with a 25565 fallback, Bedrock from the configured bedrockPort (also covers Java+Geyser cross-play), Voice fixed at 24454 gated on the per-server voice-chat-tunnel toggle.

Falls back to showing the secret-key setup sheet if no key is configured yet.

Parses the playitd daemon's log stream: extracts the agent UUID from "agent_id=..." (persisting it once learned), flags unexpected claim URLs (shouldn't appear in the secret-key flow), and extracts the tunnel address using a "tunnel setup" precursor-line state flag plus known-domain matching (joinmc.link, auto.playit.gg, ply.gg). Direct instance of the deletion test's "console log parsing" row, just for a different subprocess's log.

Calls playit.gg's /tunnels/list REST API and parses the JSON response into Java/Bedrock/Voice addresses -- Java uses the assigned domain, Bedrock/Voice use the static IP (Xbox Broadcast's RakNet transfer packet needs a real IP, not a domain). On change, resyncs Xbox Broadcast (skipped during initiation pass 2 to avoid discarding an in-progress sign-in) and re-syncs Simple Voice Chat's voice_host.

Idempotent tunnel creation with a retry loop (~16 attempts) absorbing the API's transient AgentVersionTooOld/AgentNotFound responses while the daemon is still connecting, skipping entirely if a same-named tunnel already exists.

Detects playit-enabled + Bedrock-port-configured + no Bedrock tunnel address yet, to fire a one-time "missing tunnel" alert -- explicitly suppressed during initiation pass 2 since tunnels there briefly report pending before resolving.

Writes the resolved tunnel address into Simple Voice Chat's voice_host (gated on SVC being installed). On start/agent-connect, checks whether the voice tunnel already exists (via the API) to sync, or logs that the user needs to sign in to create it -- creation itself needs a web session, not the read-only agent secret.

Full local-state reset for re-testing/switching accounts: stops the tunnel, deletes the Keychain secret and on-disk secret file, clears stored addresses. Explicitly does NOT touch the server-side agent/tunnels.

Toggles playit/voice-chat-tunnel flags per server, resets the SVC-mismatch-dismissed flag when voice turns off, and when voice chat is freshly enabled with an agent already online, decides whether to just sync (tunnel exists) or prompt sign-in (tunnel needs creating, which needs a web session).

The native account-linking workflow: signs in via the API, reuses an existing agent or claims a new one via a continuous claim-code-polling task racing an accept-with-retry loop (works around the API's WaitingForAgent state-propagation timing), exchanges for the permanent secret key, persists it, then creates Java/Bedrock/Voice tunnels as applicable. This is effectively the pairing/credential-establishment flow for a third-party tunneling service.

symbol: PlayitAPI (signin, claimSetup, postWithSession, claimAccept, claimDetails, createTunnel, tunnelExists, claimExchange, generateClaimCode)
notes: The low-level REST client for playit.gg. postWithSession brute-forces four Authorization header formats ("session X", "agent-key X", "Bearer X", raw) since the session-auth scheme isn't documented -- accepting whichever gets past an auth-type-error response. This probing behavior must be preserved verbatim in any port; getting it wrong silently breaks tunnel creation.

Detects Simple Voice Chat by jar-name sniffing in plugins/ or mods/ (checked over the config folder because MSC itself may create that folder while patching), locates voicechat-server.properties across the Paper vs Fabric/Forge/NeoForge loader-dependent paths, and surgically upserts voice_host/bind_address/port while preserving all other lines -- a targeted properties-file patcher, not a full rewrite.

Lists the backups directory, filters to .zip, reads each backup's .meta.json sidecar for slot/trigger metadata (falling back to a filename-derived auto/manual guess for legacy files), sorts newest-first, and computes the folder's total size on a background thread. makeDisplayName reconstructs a human timestamp from either the current `<level>_auto_<ts>`/`<level>_manual_<ts>` filename scheme or the legacy `<name>-<ts>` scheme.

The authoritative backup-creation implementation every other path funnels through: resolves world-slot association (explicit id, else the currently-active slot), reads level-name, prunes old auto-backups first, builds a timestamped filename with the auto/manual token, runs a flush-consistent snapshot (pausing saves only when the target IS the actively running server), zips via /usr/bin/zip, ALWAYS resumes saves afterward even on zip failure, and writes the BackupMeta sidecar on success.

Platform-specific flush-consistent snapshot protocol: Java sends `save-all flush` then `save-off`, awaiting a "Saved the game"/"Saved the world" console line (10s timeout, non-fatal); Bedrock sends `save hold` then polls `save query` until BDS reports files "ready to be copied" (10s timeout, non-fatal). A timeout still proceeds with the zip -- it's a best-effort consistency window, not a hard requirement. Saves are always re-enabled regardless of outcome.

A generic predicate-based, timeout-raced await-a-console-line primitive shared with the single console observation point (handleServerOutputLine, defined elsewhere). Race-safe single-resume via array-membership check since both the match and timeout paths run on the main actor.

Reads/writes a per-backup .meta.json sidecar (serverId, displayName, slot association, worldSeed, triggerReason), non-fatal on failure since the zip itself is the important artifact. deleteBackup removes a backup and its paired sidecar together.

Retention policy: deletes the oldest app-managed backups (matching ONLY the _auto_/_manual_ filename tokens -- explicitly never touching foreign zips a user placed in the folder) down to maxCount-1, removing orphaned sidecars alongside.

A carefully-gated destructive workflow: Java-only, refuses while the target server is running, refuses a cross-slot restore (the backup's slotId must match the currently active slot), verifies the source file exists, creates a MANDATORY safety backup first (aborting the whole restore if that fails), validates the zip is openable before touching anything, removes existing world folders, then extracts via /usr/bin/unzip. The gate ordering is safety-critical and must be preserved exactly.

Provisions a brand-new server folder from a backup: copies the template server's jar (or defaults to paper.jar), copies plugins/ and server.properties if present, writes eula=false, extracts the backup zip on top, then registers a new ConfigServer entry and sets it active. Bridges the backups and server-provisioning domains.

A near-duplicate of createBackup worth reconciling in the port rather than porting twice.
Shared helper removing <level>/<level>_nether/<level>_the_end folders, used by both Restore and Replace World.
FLAG -- a third, file-local minimal key=value .properties parser (skips comments/blank lines) duplicated from the shared ServerPropertiesManager used elsewhere.

Rebuilds the local/template/online version snapshot for the selected server (reads local Paper/Geyser/Floodgate/Broadcast versions, optionally clears online state) and triggers a plugin/mod rescan -- state aggregation the agent owns; the UI only displays componentsSnapshot.

Concurrently fetches online version info for Paper (via PaperDownloader), Geyser/Floodgate (via PluginDownloader), and Broadcast (via GitHubReleaseChecker), then fans results into the snapshot and into discoveredPlugins, followed by a user-sourced-plugin sweep. Real orchestration, not view code.

Scans the plugins/ folder, classifies each jar into managed (Geyser/Floodgate) / userSourced (has a PluginSourceConfig, matched exact-or-prefix by findSource) / unmanaged tiers, parses display name/version via PluginNameParser, preserves already-fetched online data, and sorts (managed-first, Geyser-before-Floodgate, then alpha). This tiering + jarStem-matching is a real classification policy the agent must reproduce, not a view concern.

Concurrently checks every user-sourced plugin against its configured source (GitHub / Modrinth / Hangar / direct URL), dispatching to the matching API client and URL parser per source.type. This is the plugin-update-check engine, not UI.

Paper-only online refresh (used when switching Stable/Experimental track) plus the track-switch itself, which clears selection/version list and re-triggers the fetch. No-ops if the track isn't actually changing -- a small but real guard, not just @Published plumbing.

Downloads the user-picked Paper build directly to the server's Paper jar location, creating the destination dir, then writes the version sidecar via PaperVersionSidecarManager so local version display updates immediately. Requires server-stopped; real provisioning workflow.

FLAG -- downloads and applies a specific or latest server-core jar for the flavor. Core version-management workflow with a real safety policy embedded -- this exact downgrade-guard pattern also appears in upgradeModdedLoader and updateBedrockVMFiles below (see side findings).

Determines the locally-installed Paper/plugin version: reads the PaperVersionSidecarManager sidecar first, falls back to parsing the jar filename via ComponentVersionParsing (build-number extraction from filename). Text-to-structured-data parsing, agent-owned.

Derives the installed MCXboxBroadcast version: strips the 'MCXboxBroadcastStandalone-' prefix from the configured jar's filename, or falls back to a persisted .version.txt sidecar, or reports 'Installed (version unknown)'. Filename/sidecar parsing, agent-owned.

Fetches the available Bedrock version list once (guarded so it doesn't refetch), and setBedrockVersion normalizes the picker value ('' or 'LATEST' -> nil pin) before persisting -- a real normalization policy, not just a setter.

FLAG -- VM-backend 'pull latest image' equivalent: downgrade guard (forces pre-downgrade backup, aborts on failure) then calls BedrockProvisioner.ensureInstalled(force:true) to (re)install BDS files into serverDir. Genuine provisioning workflow; third occurrence of the downgrade-guard pattern.

Small persisted library of past loader installs, deduped by record id (recordLoaderVersion), filtered by flavor, removable, and re-appliable (constructs a ServerVersionEntry and re-invokes upgradeModdedLoader). The dedup-by-id and filter are real logic, not pure forwarding.

Custom Codable implementation that decodes every field added after the initial schema via decodeIfPresent with an explicit default, so older server_config.json files never fail to decode and wipe the server list. Models a shared-access token: make() generates a UUID id + ISO8601 createdAt/optional expiresAt; isExpired compares the parsed expiry against now; init(from:) backward-compatibly defaults role to 'admin' for pre-role entries. This is pairing/token lifecycle logic (msc2-decisions calls out token lifecycle as agent-owned), not a plain data carrier.

Batch-fetches Modrinth project metadata (for server_side) for every downloadable manifest jar, chunked at 100 ids per Modrinth's batch cap, degrading gracefully (log + empty result) on a failed chunk rather than blocking the import.

Resolves 'what is the active persistent world slot' with a real fallback chain: explicit active slot if set -> most-recently-created existing slot -> create a new slot from the current live world named from level-name (capitalized) or the Bedrock level name, falling back to 'World 1'. Not a simple getter -- this is the persistent-world-identity bootstrap logic.

Saves the live world back into whatever slot ensureActiveWorldSlotExists resolves. saveCurrentWorldAsSlot is a documented legacy wrapper that intentionally now ignores its name parameter and redirects here (behavior changed from 'create new slot' to 'update active slot') -- worth preserving that semantic in the port, not just the signature.
Validates a non-empty trimmed name, then creates a brand-new fresh world slot (optionally seeded) via WorldSlotManager and reloads the slot list on completion.

Swaps the server's active world to a given slot. Refuses outright if this server is the currently running active server (a real safety policy, not just a UI disable) and always backs up the current world before swapping via WorldSlotManager.activateSlot's backupCurrent flag.

DECIDED (agent, setSlotThumbnail specifically -- see WorldSlotManager.saveThumbnail for the full reasoning, same call). Slot CRUD orchestration otherwise unchanged: deleteWorldSlot carries a real policy (refuses to delete the currently-active slot, checked via WorldSlotManager.resolvedActiveSlotID); duplicateWorldSlot/copyWorldSlot are non-destructive-copy vs destructive-overwrite variants over the same WorldSlotManager copy primitive.

Two-phase backup-into-slot restore: refuses if the backup's slotId doesn't match the target slot (wrong-slot guard) or if the server is currently the running active one; Phase 1 atomically swaps the slot's world.zip via a temp-file copy+move; Phase 2, only if the slot is currently active, takes a safety backup of the live world, deletes the current live world folders, and unzips the restored zip in their place via /usr/bin/unzip. A partial failure after Phase 1 is reported as recoverable ('re-activate the slot'). This is the most intricate single workflow in the WorldSlots file.

Import/export around the slot model: importLegacyBackupAsNewSlot validates the zip is openable then derives a proposed name (backup's slotName, else 'Imported <displayName>', else 'Imported Backup') before delegating to importZIPAsSlot, which manually constructs a new slot directory + metadata + zip-size population with rollback (removes the slot dir) on any failure. exportWorldSlot is a thin file-copy to a caller-supplied destination -- the NSSavePanel itself is explicitly documented as the UI's responsibility, not this method's.

Called after a server's first stop: if no slots exist yet but world folders are present on disk, auto-creates a persistent slot from the current world and marks it active. Idempotent (no-ops once slots exist) migration-style bootstrap for pre-slot-model servers.

Manages the global plugin-template directory: lazily creates it, lists/sorts .jar contents, copies new files in (overwriting same-named existing templates), and removes one. Template-library management the agent owns (a shared resource across all servers).

Applies selected plugin templates to the active server's plugins/ dir. Refuses while the server is running. Real replacement policy: for each template, derives a 'prefix' (text before the first '-') and removes any existing plugin jar sharing that prefix case-insensitively before copying the template in -- this is how 'Geyser-Spigot-old.jar' gets replaced by 'Geyser-Spigot-new.jar'.
Symmetric to the plugin-template trio, for the global Paper-jar template directory.

Applies a Paper template jar to the active server (server-must-be-stopped guard), resolving the destination to the configured paperJarPath or serverDir/paper.jar, replacing any existing file, and writing the PaperVersionSidecarManager sidecar by parsing the template's filename via ComponentVersionParsing so the Components tab shows the right local build even for a generic paper.jar filename.

FLAG -- downloads the latest Paper build (via PaperDownloader) into a temp file inside the template dir, then renames it to a versioned 'paper-<version>-build<build>.jar' and reloads the template list. This async version is the currently-active implementation, invoked from downloadAndApplyLatestPaper below via await -- a separate, synchronous, self-Task.detached-wrapping function of the exact same name and purpose already exists in AppViewModel+PaperTemplateDownload.swift (line 18, ledgered earlier in this batch) and appears to have zero call sites anywhere in the codebase. See side findings -- whatever earlier fixture exists for this workflow should be checked against the active async version, not the dead sync one.
Same download-into-templates pattern as Paper, for Geyser/Floodgate via PluginDownloader, with build number embedded in the final filename.

UNSURE -- builds a per-server display summary of the installed Paper/Geyser/Floodgate jars: for Geyser/Floodgate it scans plugins/ and picks the jar with the newest modification date among files whose stem has that prefix (a real 'which one is current' selection rule, not just a lookup), then formats '<filename> — <date>' strings. The selection rule is clearly agent logic, but whether the display-string formatting half should stay agent-side or move to the client once ported is genuinely open.

Per-server 'update from template' actions: pick the latest matching template (via latestTemplate below), remove old same-prefix jars from the destination, copy the new one in, and (Paper only) write the version sidecar. updateGeyserFromTemplate/updateFloodgateFromTemplate are one-line callers into the shared updatePluginTemplate helper.

Single-action 'download the latest and apply it to this server' entry points used by the Components tab: sequences a template download then the matching update-from-template call, then refreshes the local/template snapshot.

FLAG -- defines what 'latest' means when picking a template by prefix: plain lexicographic string sort on filename, last element wins (jars.sorted { $0.lastPathComponent < $1.lastPathComponent }.last). Every update-from-template call above depends on this exact rule. For filenames like 'paper-1.21.9-build5.jar' vs 'paper-1.21.10-build1.jar', string comparison does not match numeric/semver ordering -- possibly a latent bug, inherited behavior that needs an explicit port-time decision (preserve as-is vs fix to true version ordering) rather than silently carrying it forward.

Derives the initial world slot's name (requested name, else the trimmed server name, else 'World 1') and normalizes the initial seed (only meaningful for a .fresh world source; blank -> nil). Small but load-bearing precedence rules used by both createNewServer and createNewBedrockServer.

Writes level-name (and optionally level-seed) into server.properties (Java, via ServerPropertiesManager) or raw Bedrock properties (via BedrockPropertiesManager), branching on serverType -- the mechanism by which a newly created server's world identity gets pinned into its config file.

Creates the first persistent world slot for a brand-new server from any WorldSource (fresh/backupZip/existingFolder), each routing to a different WorldSlotManager factory, then updates the server's level-name/seed to match the created slot's resolved world and marks it active. Shared by both createNewServer and createNewBedrockServer.

The full Java server creation pipeline: folder layout under serversRoot/java/<slug>/, branches on flavor.provisioningKind (NeoForge/Forge run their installer; Paper/Purpur/Vanilla/Fabric go through jar-source resolution with an archive-first optimization that skips a download if the exact Paper build is already archived), writes eula.txt=false and initial server.properties (port/motd/difficulty/gamemode/level-name/seed pulled from imported-world metadata when applicable), creates the add-on folder and applies cross-play templates if requested, stages the chosen world source, constructs the ConfigServer (RAM defaults differ for modded vs plugin flavors), creates the initial world slot (aborting and cleaning up the folder if that fails), applies any wizard-staged add-ons, and rolls back the whole directory on any thrown error. This is the single most consequential workflow across all 8 files for the port.

Bedrock analogue of createNewServer: folder layout under serversRoot/bedrock/<slug>/, writes raw BDS properties + empty allowlist/permissions files, resolves the actual world folder from a user-selected import via resolvedBedrockWorldFolder, stages the world source (BDS expects worlds at serverDir/worlds/{level-name}/), constructs the ConfigServer, creates the initial world slot with the same abort-and-cleanup-on-failure pattern as the Java path.

Locates the Geyser/Floodgate jars in the global plugin-template dir and copies both into a freshly created server's plugins/ dir when cross-play was requested at creation time; logs a clear message if either template is missing rather than silently skipping.

Detects the actual Bedrock world folder (the directory containing level.dat) within a user-selected import URL, handling both 'user picked the world folder itself' and 'user picked a wrapper/parent folder containing exactly one world subfolder' shapes, falling back to the original selection if neither pattern matches. Real structural detection heuristic over Finder-selected input.

Copies a freshly-downloaded server-core jar into the shared archive dir under a versioned filename whose pattern is flavor-specific (paper-X-buildN.jar, purpur-X-buildN.jar, minecraft_server-X.jar, fabric-server-launch-X.jar); no-ops for flavors without a defined pattern (NeoForge/Forge, which archive via their own installer path). Server/core jars only -- mods are explicitly excluded from this mechanism.

Applies one wizard-staged add-on chosen during server creation, dispatching on its source: Modrinth version download, local-jar copy, arbitrary remote-URL download, .mrpack/CurseForge modpack import (delegates to importModpack, which sniffs the archive kind), or a plain zip whose top-level jars get extracted (via ditto, not unzip) and copied in. One function, six real provisioning paths.

The per-console-line dispatcher: silently consumes world-time and spark-tps-block responses (so they never reach the console display), feeds registered console-line waiters (the single observation point backups use for save-confirmation), detects server-ready state (a Paper 'Done (' line or a Bedrock 'Server started' line), triggers first-run auto-stop during Initiate pass 1, mirrors to Bedrock's log file, and fans out to every parse* function below. This is the core of 'console log parsing' the deletion test explicitly calls out as agent-owned.

Because BDS writes no log file of its own, MSC mirrors its console output into logs/latest.log, rolling the previous session to a timestamped console-<date>.log on each start and pruning to the 10 most recent rolled logs. Writes go through a serial background queue to avoid blocking the main thread during output bursts, with ordering guaranteed relative to close.

Startup-failure diagnostics: diagnoseUnexpectedStop runs StartupCrashAnalyzer off-main against the recent console excerpt for modded servers that never reached ready state, persisting a structured LastStartupResult and surfacing offender summaries; scanPaperSoftFailures does the analogous non-fatal scan for plugin load failures on a *successful* Paper start; reopenStartupProblems reloads that persisted JSON to reopen the diagnostics sheet later. The JSON decode/persist and the analysis calls are agent; only the boolean 'show sheet' flag is UI.
Extracts the running Bedrock server version from the 'Starting Minecraft Bedrock server version X' startup line.

Runs `docker info` as a subprocess with a 3-second hard timeout (force-terminates if still running) to determine daemon availability, trying /usr/local/bin/docker then falling back to /usr/bin/docker.

Parses MCXboxBroadcast's own console output: extracts the device-auth link+code from 'enter the code X at https://www.microsoft.com/link' to surface a sign-in prompt, extracts the authenticated gamertag from 'Successfully authenticated as X (xuid)' (arming a technical-wait timeout and offering to save the gamertag), and detects 'Creation of Xbox LIVE session was successful' as the broadcast-ready signal for the Initiate flow.

Delegates the actual line format detection to the (presumably already-ledgered) TpsLineParser seam, but owns the resulting state update: sets the three current TPS values and appends to a capped-at-30-samples rolling history for the Performance tab.

A small stateful parser for the multi-line `/spark tps` auto-poll reply (~9 lines): detects the header only while a block was explicitly requested (so a user's manual /spark tps still prints normally), captures the TPS values line via TpsLineParser.parseSparkValues, then swallows the CPU-usage and tick-duration sections by content/count until the block ends, with a hard 12-line safety-net cap. Returns whether each line was consumed so the caller drops it from the console display.

Parses server responses to auto-issued `time query` commands across three distinct wire formats that have changed across Minecraft versions (Paper 26+ 'The game time is X', Paper 1.21.4+ 'Timeline minecraft:day/gametime is at X ticks', and the legacy positional 'The time is X' queue where response order must be tracked via pendingTimeQueryKinds) into worldDayNumber / worldTimeOfDayTicks. Genuine multi-format parsing with a stateful fallback for the oldest format.
Extracts a numeric health value from the response to `/data get entity <name> Health` for the currently-featured player.
Parses a '<N> players online: name1, name2, ...' line into the onlinePlayers list, appends any new names to the session history, and records the count into a capped rolling history.

Parses Bedrock 'Player connected: name, xuid: X' / 'Player disconnected: name' lines, extracting gamertag+optional XUID, updating/merging the online-players list, recording session join/leave events, firing notifications, backfilling a blank-XUID allowlist entry once the XUID becomes known, persisting the XUID->name mapping to BedrockNameCache, and triggering a profile refresh. The densest single parser in the file -- extractIdentity's comma/xuid-prefix parsing plus five follow-on side effects.

Parses Java's ' joined the game' / ' left the game' suffix lines by taking the last whitespace-delimited token before the suffix as the player name, then records the session event and fires the matching notification.

When a Bedrock player connects with a known XUID, finds the matching allowlist entry that currently has a blank XUID (by case-insensitive name match) and fills it in, persisting the updated allowlist. Closes the gap where a player was allowlisted by name before their first connect.

symbol: scanWatchFolder (exact / macOS-duplicate-suffix / single-remaining-fallback filename matching) / startWatching / scheduleMove / chooseWatchFolder
notes: UNSURE -- watches a local Downloads-style folder and matches newly-appeared files against a list of expected CurseForge mod filenames (exact match, then a macOS 'name (1).ext' duplicate-suffix pattern, then a single-remaining-file fallback), moving matches into the server's mods/ directory. Contains real matching logic (the three-tier heuristic), but the entire mechanism is inherently tied to the local device: in MSC 1 the browser download and the mods/ folder are on the same Mac, so a local FileManager watch-and-move works. In MSC 2's client/agent split this doesn't map cleanly -- the download happens in the user's browser (on whatever device runs the client) while mods/ lives on the agent's machine, so 'watch local Downloads and move the file' would need to become 'client uploads the matched file to an agent endpoint' instead. Marked client because folder-watching is a local-device concern (same category as Finder/file-picker presentation), but the three-tier filename-matching algorithm itself is worth preserving conceptually if this manual-download UX survives the port -- see side findings.

FLAG -- a real component-version-comparison engine embedded in a status-pill view helper: parses a 'buildN' suffix out of a version string when present (preferring build-number comparison over the raw string), otherwise falls back to dot-separated numeric version-component comparison, and classifies local/template/online into Missing/Template mismatch/Update available/Up to date. This is domain knowledge (how to compare two component version strings) that likely overlaps with the already-fixture-covered P0.4 component-version parsing/comparison domain (fixtures/component-version/) and/or MCVersionComparator referenced elsewhere in the mixed-bucket ledger (AppViewModel+ComponentsVersions.swift's downgrade guard) -- worth an explicit cross-check against those existing fixtures rather than treating this as a wholly separate implementation to port. Everything else in this 1529-line file (toolbars, row views, sheets, badges) is routine SwiftUI wired to already-agent-owned AppViewModel methods -- client, not separately ledgered.

Checks for flavor-specific installation markers on disk (fabric-server-launch.jar, quilt-server-launch.jar, or run.sh/libraries/ for NeoForge/Forge) to decide whether a modded server's loader is actually installed yet. This is 'Server installation detection' verbatim from the deletion test's Agent column, currently duplicated here rather than reusing the mixed-bucket AppViewModel+ServerImport.detectJavaFlavor detection logic (see side findings) -- worth consolidating during the port.

Reads the configured broadcast jar's file-modification date and formats a '<filename> — <date>' display string, gated on the file actually existing on disk. Same newest-file-with-mtime-formatting pattern already ledgered as UNSURE for AppViewModel+Templates.jarSummary (mixed bucket) and duplicated again in JarsTabPluginRow.filename / JarsTabModRow.filename in this same file -- a third occurrence worth consolidating (see side findings). otherPluginEntries() (line 214) is pure view-list filtering over an already-classified list and isn't separately ledgered.

Maps an already-resolved display bullet's label prefix ('Target device', 'Java port', 'Recommended protocol', 'Bedrock port', 'Bedrock enabled') back to a RouterGuideToken case, used only to decide whether to render a cell as 'could not detect' (unresolved-token styling). Operates entirely on strings the agent-owned RouterPortForwardGuideRuntimeResolver (mixed bucket, already ledgered) has already produced -- this is UI-only reverse-lookup for highlighting, not new domain logic, so client. The rest of the file (SectionDispatcher and every *SectionView/*Row struct) is routine SwiftUI presentation of pre-resolved guide content and isn't separately ledgered.

Builds the mscremote://pair URL (base host + port + token as query items) that MSCRemoteiOS scans/opens to pair. This is the pairing wire format itself, not a view -- matches the deletion test's own worked example ('Pairing security and token lifecycle belong to the agent/API'). Belongs in the agent/API layer that also owns the token.

Decides which of this machine's own addresses to advertise for pairing: prefer a Tailscale 100.x address, else a private-range LAN address, else none. candidateIPv4Addresses enumerates local interfaces via getifaddrs (macOS-specific syscalls); isLocalOrPrivateHost classifies an address as loopback/.local/10.x/192.168.x/172.16-31.x/169.254.x. 'What address can reach me' is inherently the agent's own knowledge, not the client's -- but isLocalOrPrivateHost's range classification duplicates logic already fixture-covered by P0.14 (NetworkSafetyTests, private-range classification); the port belongs against those existing fixtures rather than re-deriving new ones.

Generates/assigns-role-to/revokes named Remote API tokens and rotates the owner's bearer token, today by mutating local AppConfig JSON directly. This is exactly the named-token permission model the deletion test names as agent-owned ('Pairing security and token lifecycle belong to the agent/API') and that D-019 says must be preserved and formalized. Target domain corresponds directly to the already-built POST /users, /users/revoke, /users/update route family (P0.23g) -- in MSC 2 this view's local mutations become calls to those routes instead of direct config writes.

Walks the app-support and servers-root directory trees (FileManager.enumerator, summing regular-file sizes) to report disk usage. Disk usage can only be measured on the machine that actually holds the files -- on a headless/remote agent the client has no filesystem access at all, so this must be an agent capability (likely a new /storage-style route; no existing route reports this today, see P0.30 notes).

symbol: loadSettings() / Save button (javaPath, extraFlags, curseForgeAPIKey, remoteAPIExposeOnLAN, useVMBedrockBackend)
notes: Reads/writes the app-level preferences that actually govern agent behavior: Java executable path + JVM flags (needed wherever Java servers are launched), the CurseForge API key (used server-side for modpack imports, stored in Keychain), whether the Remote API binds to LAN, and which Bedrock backend to use. MSC 1 exposes none of this over HTTP today -- it's local-only JSON/Keychain on the one Mac running the app -- so unlike the rest of P0.30's gap list this isn't a route MSC 1 already has; it's a route family MSC 2 will need to add. bannerColorHex and suppressQuitWarning in the same Save action are pure client cosmetics, not included here. UNSURE: preferredPairingHostInput (line 27) -- it's persisted through this same save path but only affects what host string clients see in pairing links; could be argued client-side instead.

Thin call-site: the four-step confirmation ladder (lines 328-351) is UI presentation, and the actual delete-everything behavior is entirely inside viewModel.resetApplicationForTesting() -- implemented in an AppViewModel extension, not this file, so it is out of scope for a row here. Confirmation sequencing itself is client.

Lists the server's plugins/ directory and checks installed jar filenames for 'geyser'/'floodgate' to report cross-play status (Enabled/Partial/Disabled). This is server-installation detection by direct filesystem inspection -- the deletion test's own worked example ('Server installation detection belongs to the agent'). crossPlayLabelColor (line 1032) is a pure cosmetic mapping of the resulting string to a SwiftUI Color and stays client.

Coordinates validating and persisting both the Java and Bedrock server-properties drafts in one Save action (via ServerSettingsView.validatedJavaModel/validatedBedrockModel, already the P0.23b /settings target, plus PurpurConfigManager). The validators themselves live in ServerSettingsView.swift; this function is the call site that sequences load-validate-save-refresh-draft across both server types in one place, which is real orchestration logic an agent-side settings-update handler must reproduce.

Thin call-site behind the destructive-action confirmationDialog (lines 758-768): calls viewModel.deleteServerFromDisk(withId:), implemented in an AppViewModel extension outside this file. The confirmation UX is client; the actual delete-from-disk behavior is agent but is a different file's symbol to disposition.
